title: Copenhagen, a Swedish television show and her 65th birthday
summary: Only one night in Copenhagen, a lukewarm response, and a televised show in Stockholm where she celebrated her 65th birthday.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Well, I guess I'm thinking of Copenhagen as one of the centers for American musicians.

Oh, yeh, yeh, well, we didn't -- we only did one night in Copenhagen, and that would be the first tour, we didn't go back there again. But on that first tour, we got around quite a bit. We played several towns in Germany and in Holland and a lot of times we didn't make the second time we were out, because we -- the first time we were out we were doing more or less concerts. Wherein the second time we were playing mostly clubs. There's a difference, we didn't -- the concerts weren't as successful as the club engagements. Whe concerts we played in were the kind of places where they would have a variety of entertainment, you know, like more or less the serious type music and as a jazz group it might have been a first or a new thing for them.

They didn't exactly, you know, they weren't that enthusiastic about it, and one of the things I found about some of the places, I don't know what it was but they have terrific equipment, you know, audio aids, but it was always so loud we had to tell them to put it down.
Well, that's the Rock influence, I guess.

I would think so, see, and we didn't need that, but it was fun, they had some beautiful -- we did a television show in Germany, I believe, one of the cities in Germany and their facilities were out of sight. Now there was no direction, nobody said, you know, stand over and we'll do this. They had microphones on trolleys, they could move it around, cameras all over the place and you never knew what they were shooting and so they just shot. And we viewed it afterwards and it was really terrific, the way they had put it together. Even if they had given directions, we wouldn't have understood them, you know. So they just shot away and the end product was out of sight. We viewed it afterwards and they

I hope some of that is preserved --

I would like to see it again. They probably will show it, I mean, of course you must know that their television is not commercial and in most of those cities they don't even have live television until a certain time of evening, you know, and then the news comes on and these type programs would be considered special, of course, and they have a large coverage. I know we did a television show in Stockholm and of course your Sweden, the population of Sweden is like 8,000 people, I understand -- 800,000, whatever -- 8,000 right?
No, no, it's got to be more than that.

800,000, but anyway there's only one station and of course everybody tunes in, it comes at 7 o'clock in the evening, and it starts off with the news and then of course ours was a special and I imagine at that time of the evening everybody is switched on to their television set.

And I know I did a show there, I celebrated my 65th birthday in Stockholm and the day that we went on the air I talked about it and I said I was 65 years old today and of course the announcer in Swedish gave me a rose and wished me happy birthday. So the next day I was out in the street I was walking up and down the street, I noticed everybody was looking at me and smiling and I couldn't figure out what was going on until I walked up to the -- they have a center they call Culture House where they put on free concerts in the afternoon, you know, folk music, etc., and some groups and somebody said, "Happy Birthday, Maxine." And then I realized why everybody was smiling, everybody had seen the show. You know, that was quite an experience, too.
